sections.title: Plan 14 days of individualized food and water
sections.summary: CDC recommends a two-week supply for each animal. A pet count alone cannot determine safe quantities: species, size, diet, health, and weather change the requirement.
steps: Measure each pet's usual daily food and drinking-water use and confirm the emergency target with its veterinarian. Multiply the individual amounts by 14; add separate water for bowls, cleaning, and other care.
Store the normal diet in waterproof containers, retain product labels and dates, and rotate before expiry. Include prescribed diets and species-appropriate hay or other staples where required.
Keep drinking water separate from human supplies in the inventory. Pack bowls, feeding instructions, and a manual can opener if needed; identify an alternate supplier before disruption.

Store dry food and unopened cans cool and dry, below 80°F (27°C). Promptly refrigerate unused opened wet food at 40°F (4°C) or below, or discard it; without safe refrigeration use meal-sized packs. Keep the original label, lot and date.
warnings: Do not ration essential drinking water to make an estimate last. Do not substitute one species' diet for another or make a therapeutic-diet change without veterinary advice.

sections.title: Prepare medicines and a veterinary care plan
sections.summary: A written plan helps another caregiver continue essential treatment without guessing doses or storage rules.
steps: Ask the veterinarian about a two-week medicine supply where appropriate and lawful, refill timing, required supplies, and a product-specific temperature plan. Keep original labels and rotate stock.
Write the pet's condition, current prescribed dose and schedule, allergies, feeding needs, and emergency warning signs supplied by its veterinarian. Record doses as given.

Identify a usual and alternate emergency clinic, including one outside the disruption area. Ask about missed doses, failed refrigeration, and how to authorize treatment if someone else evacuates the animal.
warnings: Do not give human medicines or another animal's prescription unless a veterinarian specifically directs their use for this animal. Breathing trouble, collapse, seizures, serious injury, or suspected poisoning requires urgent veterinary help; do not wait for supplies to run out.

sections.title: Practice evacuation with cats and dogs
sections.summary: Prearrange a destination, transport, and a backup caregiver. Confirm the destination accepts the animals you actually have.
steps: Keep labeled carriers or crates and leashes near the exit. Practice loading every animal and the kit; arrange an accessible ride if you have no vehicle.
For cats, use a secure carrier, familiar bedding, and a litter plan. Know hiding places and begin gathering animals early. Open the carrier only inside a secure room.

For dogs, use a fitted harness or collar and leash for transfers, a suitable secured crate or vehicle restraint, and planned toileting stops. A housing crate must allow standing and turning comfortably.
Confirm shelter or boarding rules, vaccine documentation, and whether animals are housed separately. A pet-friendly plan and a service-animal access plan may have different arrangements.
warnings: Take pets when you evacuate; do not leave them chained outside. Frightened animals may bite or escape. Do not allow animals to ride loose or leave them alone in a parked vehicle.

sections.title: Adapt the plan for small pets, birds, and reptiles
sections.summary: A cat-and-dog kit does not meet every species' housing, food, temperature, or equipment needs. Prepare a species-specific plan with a veterinarian familiar with that animal.
steps: Use a secure, ventilated transport enclosure appropriate to the species; inspect doors and surfaces for escape or chewing risks. Label the enclosure and keep compatible groups only as advised.
For small mammals, pack the usual diet, appropriate bedding, water-delivery equipment, and any required hay. Reduce handling and keep transport quiet, separated from predators.

For birds, plan a secure travel cage and species-appropriate food and environmental protection. For reptiles, amphibians, or fish, plan safe transport and the exact temperature, water-quality, power, and habitat support required.
Rehearse the setup at the destination. Identify when loss of habitat control makes early relocation necessary.
warnings: Do not use universal food, fluid, medicine doses, or temperature targets across species. Avoid unattended improvised heaters; contact an appropriate veterinarian for illness or loss of essential habitat support.

sections.title: Keep animals and people clean in shared shelter
sections.summary: Pet waste, food, and damaged environments can spread germs. Plan cleaning water and supplies as well as drinking water.
steps: Wash hands with soap and safe water after handling animals, food, cages, or waste. Keep pet-care supplies away from food preparation and protect open wounds from licking.
Pack a litter tray and litter for cats, waste bags for dogs, and suitable enclosure-cleaning supplies for small pets. Remove waste promptly and follow local disposal instructions.
Clean bowls, cages, and bedding regularly. Use products suitable for the species and surface exactly as labeled; keep animals away until the product permits return.
Keep pets away from floodwater, stagnant water, wildlife, and unfamiliar animals. On return, check for chemicals, sharp debris, damaged fences, and exposed wiring.
warnings: Never mix cleaning chemicals. Stress can change behavior; handle gently and report bites for medical assessment. A sick animal needs veterinary advice and separation as directed.

sections.title: Maintain safe temperatures and recognize distress
sections.summary: Temperature tolerance varies with species, age, coat, body condition, and illness. Plan relocation before heating or cooling fails.
steps: Ask the veterinarian for the animal's safe environment and warning signs. Keep pets sheltered, dry, and supervised, with fresh water and shade where appropriate; never leave a pet in a parked car.
During heat, reduce exertion and walk dogs in cooler hours, avoiding hot pavement. Watch for excessive panting or drooling, unsteadiness, abnormal gums, and collapse; seek emergency veterinary care.

During cold, provide dry bedding and an appropriate warm indoor location. Keep drinking water from freezing and shorten necessary outdoor trips. Monitor vulnerable and habitat-dependent animals closely.
Move early to a pet-accepting safe location if suitable temperature cannot be maintained. Keep heaters guarded and follow manufacturer fire clearances.
warnings: Collapse, abnormal breathing, severe shivering, weakness, or altered responsiveness requires urgent veterinary help. Do not assume fur makes an animal safe in extreme temperatures.

sections.title: Prepare identification, records, and reunification
sections.summary: Current identification and paper records help reunite animals with owners and let temporary caregivers provide appropriate care.
steps: Check collar tags where appropriate and confirm microchip registration details. Add an out-of-area contact; label carriers with the pet's name and reachable owner information.

Keep recent photos, including a photo with the owner, a physical description, proof of ownership, microchip details, vaccination records, and medical instructions in a waterproof packet. Keep a second accessible copy.
List the veterinarian, emergency clinic, animal control, shelters, boarding destination, and backup caregiver. Share the care plan with the person who may collect the animal.
If separated, get people to safety first, notify local shelters and animal control, and tell the microchip registry. Check official local lost-animal arrangements repeatedly as new animals arrive.
warnings: A microchip is identification, not a live location tracker. Familiar landmarks may change after disaster; continue leash or carrier control even near home.

sections.title: Protect pets from CO, smoke, and unsafe food
sections.summary: The same combustion hazards that threaten people also poison animals. Food storage and pet-safe shelter matter throughout an outage.
steps: Use battery-backed CO alarms. Run generators outdoors more than 20 feet from doors, windows, and vents; never use grills, camp stoves, or vehicle engines inside a home or garage.

If a CO alarm sounds or poisoning is suspected, move people and pets outside immediately, call 911 from safety, and seek veterinary advice for exposed animals. Do not re-enter until responders say it is safe.
Reduce smoke exposure and follow evacuation orders. A particle filter does not remove CO, and a pet carrier does not protect against toxic air.

Use the normal safe diet, follow food storage labels, and discard contaminated or recalled food. Keep fresh or opened refrigerated products cold as directed; ask the veterinarian about an appropriate shelf-stable alternative before an outage. CDC discourages raw diets for cats and dogs.
warnings: Do not feed flood-exposed or spoiled food, assume freezing sterilizes raw food, or rely on smell to detect CO. Breathing difficulty or collapse is an emergency.

kit.name: 14-day normal food supply
kit.detail: Individual quantities confirmed for each animal; include prescribed diets and required species-specific staples, with dates and feeding instructions.

kit.name: 14-day individualized drinking water
kit.detail: Use usual consumption and veterinary advice; add separate cleaning water and extra needs. Record usable liters rather than assuming one allowance fits all pets.

kit.name: Bowls and feeding equipment
kit.detail: Pack non-spill bowls, the usual water bottle or feeder where needed, food scoop, and manual can opener for canned food.

kit.name: Medicines and administration supplies
kit.detail: Ask about two weeks of prescribed medicines, labeled instructions, necessary measuring supplies, and product-specific temperature protection. Keep a dose log.

kit.name: Labeled carrier or crate for every animal
kit.detail: Choose secure ventilation and species-appropriate construction and space; practice loading and safe vehicle transport before an evacuation.

kit.name: Leash, harness, and identification
kit.detail: Pack suitable fitted restraints and backups for cats or dogs as appropriate; label enclosures and keep microchip registration current.

kit.name: Waste and enclosure-cleaning supplies
kit.detail: Include litter and tray, dog waste bags, appropriate small-pet bedding, paper towels, trash bags, soap, and species-safe cleaning products.

kit.name: Waterproof medical and ownership records
kit.detail: Vaccinations, medical summary, prescriptions, chip details, physical description, recent photos, proof of ownership, and care authorization where appropriate.

kit.name: Paper care and evacuation contacts
kit.detail: Usual and alternate veterinarian, emergency clinic, accepting destination, transport helper, backup caregiver, animal control, and local shelters.

kit.name: Familiar bedding and comfort items
kit.detail: Pack manageable dry bedding, a familiar toy, and species-appropriate comfort items; keep the rest area quiet and protect ventilation.

kit.name: Veterinarian-approved first-aid kit
kit.detail: Ask what suits each animal and your training. Keep gloves, suitable clean dressings, instructions, and emergency contacts; first aid does not replace veterinary care.

kit.name: Habitat and temperature backup plan
kit.detail: Include required species-specific transport and monitoring equipment, safe approved power options, and a relocation trigger if essential habitat conditions cannot be maintained.
